text: Renee had been told to wait in the corridor outside the imaging suite, so she sat on a vinyl chair beneath a poster about hand hygiene and tried to read the same paragraph of news on her phone three times. Across from her a man in a work fleece was bouncing one knee. Her husband had gone to find coffee an hour earlier and had not come back. She was afraid of what the radiologist would say, and afraid of the word they had used on the phone, which was "concerning," a word that sounded chosen by someone who did not want to be held responsible for it. Her mother had died of something similar at fifty-six. Renee was fifty-one. Each time the double doors opened her pulse jumped into her throat. A nurse called a name that wasn't hers, and the fear settled lower, into her stomach, where it stayed. When her husband finally appeared with two paper cups and a face she could not read, she stood up too quickly and the room tilted. She told herself to breathe. She did not yet know whether she was about to hear the worst news of her life, only that she would hear it soon.

Title: Got a letter from the IRS and I'm terrified

Long-time lurker, first post. Last month I got a letter saying my 2022 return has been selected for examination. It's a correspondence audit so it's just paperwork, I think. But the letter has a 30-day deadline and asks for documentation of a home office deduction I claimed while freelancing. I'm scared because I'll be honest: I was sloppy. I didn't keep a separate phone bill, and I'm not sure the square footage I put down was right.

My partner says I'm catastrophizing and should just gather receipts. I know that's reasonable. But I can't sleep, my heart races every time an envelope with a government return address shows up, and I've started dreading the mail, which is a weird thing to admit at 42.

Has anyone been through this with a small self-employed return? Did you pay a CPA to represent you, and roughly what did it cost? I'm nervous about the fees but more afraid of making things worse by handling it badly. Any advice on what to put in the response letter would help. I'm trying not to panic, but I'm afraid I'll end up owing far more than I can pay.

Dear Helen,

Thank you for taking my call on Tuesday, even though you were in the middle of the budget review. I know I sounded calmer than I was. The truth is I am frightened about the layoffs. Our division's name was on the list that went to finance, and nobody has told us anything directly. I'm afraid for my team, particularly Tomas, who has two kids and a mortgage in a city where nothing else pays what we do.

I also have a fear of my own that I haven't said out loud. I'm fifty-eight, and if I lose this job I am not sure I'll find another one in this industry at my level. Every time my phone buzzes after seven at night, I feel my stomach drop.

I'm not writing to ask you to change anything. I know you can't. I wanted to put the worry on paper so it stops circling my head. Would you be willing to tell me honestly what you hear in the hallway? Even bad news is easier to plan around than the silence.

With respect and gratitude,
Walter

Oct 9. Checked the lock on the back door three times before bed. The dog sat at the top of the stairs, ears up, staring at nothing. Heard a car idle on the street around two and stayed on the landing with the phone in my hand, thumb over the emergency number, not dialing. Turned on every light in the house. Sent Anna a text: are you up. She replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which I know means she's asleep. Pulled the living room curtains shut, then opened them again because I couldn't see the street. The neighbor's motion light clicked on and off for twenty minutes. Walked the perimeter with a flashlight in my socks. Found the gate latch loose, tightened it, then stood there holding the wrench longer than I needed to. Wrote the new code on a sticky note and put it inside the pantry door. Didn't sleep. At six the paper came, and I read the local section standing at the window with the lights still on.

Priscilla had driven the same route to the clinic for six years, but tonight she took the highway instead, watching the mirror for headlights that stayed too long. The trial date had been moved again. The man who had sent the letters had her new address written on his notepad; his lawyer had mentioned it as if it were a courtesy. She checked the deadbolt, then the one above it, then the window over the sink whose latch had never quite caught. In the closet she kept a duffel packed with a change of clothes, the passport in its plastic sleeve, and a kitchen knife wrapped in a dish towel, which she unwrapped, looked at, and wrapped again. Her daughter had asked why the porch light was on in the middle of the day. Priscilla had said it was a bulb, nothing more. Nobody in the building knew what she had testified about in March. At two in the morning she heard the stairwell door sigh shut, slow footsteps, then nothing. She stood in the dark kitchen with her palm flat on the cold counter, listening.
